entry: Amount of money that buyers pay for a good or service. In modern economies prices are generally quoted in [[Currency|currency]], although vouchers such as trading stamps and air miles are sometimes used as prices. Prices are shaped by production costs and by supply and demand, and a monopolist may set them or market conditions may impose them. Economic price theory holds that in a free market the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded. [[Milton Friedman]] identified five functions of prices, including transmitting information about changes in the relative importance of products and rationing fixed supplies among consumers. [[Adam Smith]] described the diamond-water paradox: diamonds command a higher price than water, although water is essential to life. Where a raw material is sold in several locations, the law of one price is generally believed to hold, so price differences should not exceed shipping and other distribution costs.

Novel of manners by English author [[Jane Austen]], published in 1813. Austen wrote it at about age 20 or 21, and it was the second of her novels to appear in print. *Pride and Prejudice* follows Elizabeth Bennet, who learns the repercussions of hasty judgments and comes to appreciate the difference between superficial goodness and actual goodness. The Bennet family's estate, Longbourn in [[Hertfordshire]], is entailed to a male heir, so one of the five daughters must marry well to support the others. Elizabeth rejects a proposal from Mr. Darcy, influenced by George Wickham's claim that Darcy had mistreated him. The novel has consistently ranked among the most-loved books of literary scholars and readers, with over 20 million copies sold. It has inspired many derivatives, including films, television versions and unofficial sequels.

Religious leader authorized to perform the sacred rituals of a religion, especially as a mediator between humans and deities. Priests administer religious rites, including sacrifices to a deity or deities, and their duties often include hearing confessions, giving spiritual direction, teaching the faith and visiting the sick. Priests exist in many religions, including branches of [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]], [[Buddhism]], [[Shinto]] and [[Hinduism]]. They are generally regarded as having privileged contact with the deity, and in some faiths the role is chosen by election; in Judaism the priesthood is inherited in familial lines. In a [[Theocracy|theocracy]], society is governed by its priesthood. The word ultimately derives, via Latin and Greek, from presbyter, the Greek term for an elder.

Colorant or colored light that can be mixed in varying amounts to produce a range of colors. The most common mixing models are additive, which uses red, green and blue light in displays, and subtractive, which uses [[Cyan|cyan]], [[Magenta|magenta]] and [[Yellow|yellow]] pigments in printing and painting. Red, yellow and blue are commonly taught as primaries in art education, despite criticism that they lack a scientific basis. Trichromatic theory, proposed by [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] in 1802 and refined by [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], holds that human color vision relies on three receptor types. No set of real colorants or lights can mix all possible colors, and no single set of primaries is canonical. Pigments and light sources are chosen for practical factors such as cost, stability and availability.

First stage of formal education, after preschool or kindergarten and before [[Secondary education|secondary education]]. It typically lasts three to six years, although in the United States the first seven to nine years of schooling are considered primary. Programs are designed to provide fundamental [[Reading|reading]], [[Writing|writing]] and mathematics skills. The 1997 International Standard Classification of Education described primary education as normally starting between ages 5 and 8 and giving an elementary understanding of other subjects; by 2011 the aim was a solid foundation for learning. The [[UNICEF|United Nations Children's Fund]] holds that primary education decreases poverty and child mortality and encourages [[Gender equality|gender equality]]. Religious communities provided early education, and in the mid-17th century Massachusetts became the first colony to mandate schooling.

Line of [[Longitude|longitude]] at which longitude is defined to be 0°. Together with its anti-meridian at 180°, it divides [[Earth|Earth]] into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Unlike the [[Equator|equator]], the prime meridian is astronomically arbitrary, and historically different regions used different conventions. [[Ptolemy]] was the first geographer to use a consistent meridian for a world map, basing it on islands in the Atlantic. The Greenwich meridian was adopted as the international standard at a conference in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D.C.]] in 1884, by 22 votes to 1 with 2 abstentions, since about two-thirds of the world's shipping already used Greenwich-based charts. Earth's current standard is the IERS Reference Meridian, which is derived from Greenwich but differs slightly.

Theorem describing the asymptotic distribution of [[Prime number|prime numbers]] among the positive integers. It states that the prime-counting function π(x), the number of primes less than or equal to x, is asymptotically equivalent to x / log x, in the sense that their ratio approaches 1 as x grows without bound. Consequently the average gap between consecutive primes among the first N integers is roughly log N. [[Adrien-Marie Legendre|Legendre]] and [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]] proposed approximating formulas that imply this equivalence, and [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] also studied the question. Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin proved the theorem independently in 1896, using ideas introduced by [[Bernhard Riemann]], particularly the [[Riemann zeta function]]. Among positive integers of at most 1000 digits, about one in 2300 is prime.

Family of herbaceous and woody [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], commonly called the primrose family. Most species are perennial, although the scarlet pimpernel is an annual. The family was once one of three in the order Primulales. Molecular phylogenetic studies led the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group to submerge that order in an enlarged order Ericales, and the original family became subfamily Primuloideae within an enlarged Primulaceae. Flowers are bisexual and radially symmetrical, with a stamen opposite each petal, and the ovules are attached to a central axis without partitions. [[Leaf|Leaves]] are simple and usually lack stipules, often forming a rosette at the base of the stem. Seeds develop in capsules that split apart to release them, and the family includes garden favorites and wildflowers.

German-born prince and husband of [[Queen Victoria]]. He married his first cousin Victoria in 1840 and was her consort until his death. Victoria granted him the title Prince Consort in 1857. Initially constrained by a role without power, he gained a reputation for supporting educational reform and the worldwide abolition of slavery. He organized the Great Exhibition of 1851, ran the Queen's household and estates, and persuaded Victoria to be less partisan in dealings with Parliament, aiding the development of [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]]. Their eldest son later succeeded as [[Edward VII]].

Island province of Canada, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. It is the smallest Canadian province by land area and population, yet has the highest population density, and it is the only province consisting entirely of islands. Its capital is Charlottetown. Ceded to Britain at the end of the [[Seven Years' War|Seven Years' War]], the island was part of Nova Scotia before becoming a separate colony in 1769. It joined Canadian Confederation as the seventh province in 1873. Farming is central to the economy: the island produces 25% of Canada's [[Potato|potatoes]], and fisheries and tourism are also important.

Paris-born military commander in the service of Austria and the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. Eugene was raised at the court of Louis XIV. Denied a commission in the French army, he entered the service of Emperor Leopold I, cousin and rival of Louis XIV, and distinguished himself during the Ottoman siege of [[Vienna]] in 1683. His victory at Zenta in 1697 ended the Ottoman threat for nearly 20 years. In the [[War of the Spanish Succession|War of the Spanish Succession]] he partnered with the Duke of Marlborough, winning at Blenheim, Oudenaarde and Malplaquet, and he later won at Petrovaradin in 1716 and at [[Belgrade]] in 1717. He also held senior office at the imperial court in Vienna, spending six decades in the service of three emperors.

Portuguese prince and patron of maritime exploration. Henry was the third child of King John I, who founded the House of Aviz, and he is often credited as one of the main initiators of the [[Age of Discovery|Age of Discovery]]. Using the new caravel ship, he directed the early development of Portuguese exploration of western Africa, the Atlantic islands and the search for new routes. He supported his father's 1415 conquest of [[Ceuta]], a Muslim port across the Strait of Gibraltar from the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. Under his sponsorship, Portuguese explorers passed Cape Bojador in 1434 and reached the Senegal River by 1445, and ventures secured trade in gold, pepper and enslaved Africans. His expeditions yielded no sea route to India during his lifetime, but they advanced navigation and laid foundations for the [[Portuguese Empire|Portuguese empire]].

American singer, songwriter, musician and filmmaker. Often credited as one of the greatest musicians of his generation, Prince pioneered the [[Minneapolis|Minneapolis]] sound and influenced genres including [[Funk|funk]], rock and pop. Born and raised in Minneapolis, he signed a record deal with Warner Bros. Records at 18 and released his first album, *For You*, two years later. In 1984 he became the first singer to have a number-one film, album and single in the United States at the same time, with *Purple Rain*, its soundtrack and "When Doves Cry". The album spent 24 consecutive weeks at number one on the U.S. Billboard 200. Prince's estimated sales exceed 100 million records. In 1993, during a contract dispute with Warner Bros., he changed his name to an unpronounceable symbol, and he reverted to Prince in 2000. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2004.

British princess, younger daughter of King [[George VI]] and sister of [[Elizabeth II]]. She was second in line to the throne until her sister's children were born. In 1955 she renounced marriage to Group Captain Peter Townsend, a divorced equerry, citing royal duties and the [[Church of England]]'s ban on remarrying divorced people. In 1960 she married photographer Antony Armstrong-Jones at [[Westminster Abbey]]; they had two children and divorced in 1978. She was patron or president of more than 80 organizations, with an emphasis on children's welfare, ballet and music. Heavy smoking and drinking contributed to [[Stroke|strokes]] from 1998.

1997 Japanese animated epic historical fantasy film by [[Hayao Miyazaki]], produced by Toshio Suzuki and animated by [[Studio Ghibli]]. It follows Ashitaka, a young Emishi prince who is drawn into a conflict between a town and the forest gods, exploring [[Environmentalism|environmentalism]] and human expansion. With a budget of ¥2.35 billion, it was the most expensive animated film of its time. Released in Japan by [[Toho]] on July 12, 1997, it became the country's highest-grossing film. Miramax distributed an English-dubbed version, with a translation by [[Neil Gaiman]]. The film has grossed US$231.3 million as of 2026.

Private [[Ivy League|Ivy League]] research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of nine colonial colleges chartered before the [[American Revolution|American Revolution]]. It officially became a university and took its present name in 1896. Its endowment of $42.3 billion is the largest per student in the United States. The university has about 9,000 students on a 600-acre campus and uses a residential college system, with eating clubs for upperclassmen. Nassau Hall hosted the Continental Congress during the Revolution. As of October 2025, 81 Nobel laureates and 16 [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]] had been affiliated with the university.

Linear technique for reducing the dimensionality of data. The data are transformed onto a new coordinate system in which the principal components, the directions capturing the largest variation, can be identified. Each component is the direction of a line that best fits the points while being orthogonal to the previous ones, and the components are uncorrelated. Many studies plot the first two components to identify clusters of related data points. PCA is applied in population genetics, microbiome studies and [[Atmospheric science|atmospheric science]]. The method originated with [[Karl Pearson]]'s 1901 work on lines and planes of closest fit to points in space.

Physics principle that the laws of physics take the same form in all inertial frames of reference. [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo Galilei]] articulated it for classical mechanics in the 17th century, using the example of a ship sailing smoothly on calm seas. In 1905 [[Albert Einstein]] extended the principle to all laws of physics, including electromagnetism, and combined it with the constancy of the speed of light for all observers, the basis of [[Special relativity|special relativity]]. In special relativity, [[Maxwell's equations|Maxwell's equations]] take the same form in all inertial frames. Einstein's 1915 [[General relativity|general relativity]] extended the principle to accelerated frames and gravity, which it interpreted as the curvature of spacetime. The principle implies that absolute motion does not appear in any law of physics.

Flat board that supports and connects electronic components. A printed circuit board (PCB) is a laminated structure of conductive and insulating layers, in which [[Copper|copper]] traces are etched from sheets bonded to a non-conductive substrate, often fiberglass-reinforced [[Epoxy|epoxy]]. Components are attached to conductive pads, generally by [[Soldering|soldering]], which both connects and fastens them. Boards with more than one side use vias, metal-lined drilled holes that connect the layers. Nearly all electronic products use PCBs, which require design effort but allow manufacturing and assembly to be automated. German inventor Albert Hanson received a patent in 1903 for a flat conductive foil laminated between insulating layers, and Paul Eisler developed the modern etched board in England in 1936, first applied in military radios during World War II.

Computer peripheral that makes a durable representation of text or graphics, usually on paper. Types include [[3D printing|3D]] printers, [[Ink|inkjet]], [[Laser|laser]] and thermal printers, as well as impact printers that strike an inked ribbon against the paper. Mechanical prototypes date to [[Charles Babbage]]'s designs for his Difference Engine in the 19th century. The first practical computer printers appeared in the 1950s, including the [[IBM|IBM]] 1403 line printer, which could output up to 1,100 lines per minute. Laser printers, commercialized by Xerox in 1977, dominate office use for their speed and precision. Modern printers often combine scanning, copying and faxing, and connect through networks or [[Wi-Fi|Wi-Fi]].

Machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto paper, cloth or a similar material. It was a major improvement on methods in which paper was rubbed by hand. German goldsmith [[Johannes Gutenberg]] invented the printing press around 1440, using movable metal type cast from a lead alloy, an adjustable wooden frame and oil-based ink. Its spread across Europe brought mass communication, lowered the cost of printed texts and raised adult literacy rates. Books increasingly appeared in vernacular languages rather than [[Latin|Latin]]. The press contributed to the [[Reformation|Reformation]], through the spread of [[Martin Luther]]'s writings, and to the [[Scientific Revolution|Scientific Revolution]]. By 1500 it had enabled the printing of over 20 million books.

Process of creating artworks by printing, normally on [[Paper|paper]] but also on fabric, [[Wood|wood]], [[Metal|metal]] and other surfaces. Prints are made by transferring ink from a matrix to a sheet of paper or other material. Common matrices include metal plates for [[Engraving|engraving]], etching and intaglio; stone or polymer for lithography; wood blocks for woodcuts; linoleum for linocuts; and silk or synthetic screens for screen printing. Except in monotyping, printmaking can produce identical multiples, each called an impression rather than a copy. Multiple impressions from one matrix form an edition. Since the late 19th century artists have generally signed and numbered impressions, often as a limited edition, after which the matrix is destroyed. A print that copies another work, especially a painting, is a reproductive print.

Infectious, misfolded protein that causes fatal neurodegenerative diseases. Prions induce normal variants of the same protein to misfold, and the term derives from proteinaceous infectious particle. Unlike [[Virus|viruses]], [[Bacteria|bacteria]] and fungi, prions contain no nucleic acids, [[DNA|DNA]] or [[RNA|RNA]]. The prion protein (PrP) occurs naturally, and its twisted forms are prions. Prion diseases affect animals and humans, including scrapie in sheep, chronic wasting disease in deer, [[Bovine spongiform encephalopathy|bovine spongiform encephalopathy]] in cattle and [[Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease|Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease]] in humans. All known prion diseases in mammals affect the brain or neural tissue, are progressive and are invariably fatal. Prions resist heat, radiation and disinfectants, which complicates decontamination. Stanley Prusiner proposed the prion hypothesis and received the 1997 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine.

Transparent optical element with flat, polished surfaces that [[Refraction|refract]] light. At least one surface must be angled, since elements with only two parallel surfaces are windows. The most familiar type is the triangular prism. Prisms are made from transparent materials such as glass, acrylic and [[Fluorite|fluorite]]. A dispersive prism splits white light into its spectral colors, the colors of the [[Rainbow|rainbow]], a phenomenon demonstrated by Isaac Newton. In spectrometers, prisms measure the minimum deviation angle of each wavelength to analyze the composition of light. Other prisms reflect light or split it into components with different [[Polarization (waves)|polarizations]], and they are used in [[Binoculars|binoculars]], periscopes and laser equipment.

Facility where people are confined by the state, usually as punishment for [[Crime|crimes]]. Prisons hold people awaiting [[Trial|trial]] and those who have been convicted and are serving sentences. They aim at incapacitation, retribution, deterrence and rehabilitation. The modern prison system emerged in the late 18th and early 19th centuries in Europe and North America, replacing public executions and corporal punishments. Early models such as the [[Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]] system of solitary confinement sought penitence. Authoritarian regimes sometimes use prisons to detain political opponents without fair trial, which is illegal under most [[International law|international law]]. The [[United States|United States]] incarcerates over 2 million people, about 500 per 100,000 residents, the highest rate in the world.
